title: Low-cost and representative surrogate hydrological models. Part I-Construction of surrogates
contribution: Builds three reduced-fidelity surrogates of the HYDROTEL hydrological model (fewer meteorological stations, shorter calibration period, fewer RHHU sub-basins) and their combination, and evaluates each by rank/value correlation with the original on 5,000 LHS points and by a binned CPU-time ratio, as Part I of a DDS-MADS calibration project.
problem_entry: Application cost: one HYDROTEL run can exceed a minute and calibration needs thousands; reduced-fidelity surrogates are underused in water resources; a good surrogate is defined by two mandatory conditions, representativeness and CPU-time decrease (pp. 4-6, 8).
key_idea: Simplify the simulator itself (checkerboard station removal, 12-month period, coarser discretization), judge surrogates by Spearman rank correlation and optimal-zone alignment alongside R2, and bin the speed-up ratio r into unusable/poor/medium/superior/ideal (pp. 8-10, 17).
assumptions: Objective 1-NSE; HYDROTEL 10 and 19 formulations on three Quebec watersheds; 0.9 threshold for R2 and Rs borrowed from Toal (2015) with the caveat that it was meant for response-surface surrogates; CPU time averaged over 1,000 runs (pp. 6-8, 10-11).
proof_devices: none (no theorems); mechanistic explanation of speed-ups from the simulator's three-step computing pipeline and hydrograph recomputation (pp. 7, 10, 16)
experiments: 5,000 LHS points per surrogate; best/worst instances per reduction level on the worst watershed (Toulnustouc); failures reported (Rs 0.638/R2 0.411 worst station instance, 6-month periods <= 0.512/0.392); combined ratios 44/16/32 for HYDROTEL 10 vs about 2 for HYDROTEL 19; 3/6 combined surrogates below 0.9 (pp. 12-19). Tables and figures not in extracted text.
positioning: Builds on Razavi et al.'s four avenues and surveys (adds hardware progress as a fifth), Le Digabel's adaptive/non-adaptive surrogate distinction and Audet & Hare's surrogate definition; fills the water-resources gap on reduced-fidelity models (pp. 5-6).
writing: Operational definitions first (two mandatory conditions, five named ratio bands), predictions of each surrogate's ratio stated before results, open questions explicitly deferred to Part II (pp. 8-10, 20).
limits_future: HYDROTEL 19 ratios poor and half the combined surrogates below 0.9; Part II to test whether R2>0.9 and an ideal ratio are needed; reduced models might serve as operational models (pp. 18-20).

title: Binary, unrelaxable and hidden constraints in blackbox optimization
contribution: Merges unrelaxable and hidden constraints into one binary constraint, models binary constraints with weighted kNN (Epanechnikov kernel) classification surrogates, and uses seven surrogate constraint-violation functions (unscaled and max-violation-scaled) to order MADS trial points, improving data profiles over the extreme barrier default in NOMAD 3.8.0 (read as GERAD G-2019-76).
problem_entry: Semantic/mechanism mismatch: binary constraints are relaxable by definition yet MADS treats them with the extreme barrier like unrelaxable/hidden ones, discarding information (p. 5).
key_idea: Replace x in X by a single unquantifiable binary b0, build kNN surrogates b~_i, and use surrogate h~ (h~1-h~7) with surrogate f~ only to reorder candidates under the opportunistic strategy, leaving PB acceptance and theory unchanged (pp. 6-9).
assumptions: No smoothness assumptions; h uses squared violations to avoid adding nonsmoothness; b0 unquantifiable by construction (pp. 6-7).
proof_devices: no theorem; claim that changing the evaluation order leaves the PB convergence analysis intact (p. 6)
binary identity max(0,b_i)^2 = b_i to simplify h (p. 7)
scaling by largest violation observed so far a_i^k (p. 8)
experiments: STYRENE (4 binary + hidden, ~14% failures, 7 relaxable), MDO and Lockwood with constraints converted to binary/unrelaxable; 30 instances each (difference not stated); NOMAD 3.8.0 OrthoMADS + quadratic models, 1500 evals; data profiles tau=1e-2,1e-4 vs own default only (pp. 9-11).
positioning: Uses Le Digabel-Wild constraint taxonomy; cites Choi et al. for hidden constraints and a modified DIRECT (Na et al.) as the other treatment; builds on PB and on the companion constraint-scaling report (pp. 5-6, 8, 11).
writing: Short letter; honest hedging of effect sizes ('minimal', 'not significant') and a concrete recommendation (h~7) (p. 11).
limits_future: Differences between variants minimal, weighting gain not significant; future: use surrogate probability of binary relaxable constraints inside the true h (p. 11).

method_links.note: refines the taxonomy (binary = relaxable but unquantifiable; unrelaxable+hidden merged into an unquantifiable binary) and gives the class its own mechanism

title: Monotonic grey box direct search optimization: C. Audet et al.
contribution: Defines monotonic grey-box optimization, develops cone-monotonicity results for extended-real functions, encodes user knowledge in a trend matrix with strict and relaxed trend directions, and uses them to order MADS poll points (with a parameter-free switch to model ordering) to reach feasibility faster, tested on analytic problems, MDO and Rio Tinto's Kemano blackbox (read as GERAD G-2019-15 'Monotonic grey box optimization').
problem_entry: Rio Tinto engineers reached feasibility on Kemano faster by hand than NOMAD from an infeasible start, because they knew which variables to move; formalized as known sign / unknown magnitude of constraint variation (pp. 4-5, 12-14).
key_idea: Trend matrix T (entries -1, 1, 0, N/A) -> trend cones -> strict trend direction d_T (zero on any N/A) and trend direction d~_T (ignores N/A); order poll candidates by angle with -d_T, switch to models once n+1 affinely independent nearby points exist (pp. 7-10).
assumptions: Cone-monotonicity for functions into R with +-infinity (failed evaluations = infinity); no differentiability or continuity; Prop. 3 needs -d_T feasible for X and upper semicontinuous satisfied constraints; sampled T only a conjecture (pp. 5-6, 9, 11).
proof_devices: two-step chaining to extend monotonicity from cones K1, K2 to conv{K1,K2} (Prop. 2, p. 6)
bridge cone-monotonicity -> Clarke derivative g°(x;d) >= 0 (Cor. 2, p. 6)
componentwise case analysis placing d_T in every violated constraint's trend cone (Cor. 4, p. 8)
split h = S_J + S_Jbar: violated part monotone along the cone, satisfied part zero nearby by upper semicontinuity (Prop. 3, p. 9; yields non-increase)
experiments: NOMAD 3.9.1, quadratic-model search off, 2n directions, minimize h until feasible; 8 analytic problems x 10 infeasible starts x 10 seeds; MDO with T sampled from 200 LHS points; Kemano (90 s/eval, budget 100, 20 starts, engineer vs sampled T); data profiles of feasibility; negative result on strict direction (d_T(x0)=0 for 18/20) reported (pp. 10-13).
positioning: Extends Van Dyke et al.'s cone-monotonicity to extended reals; cites Borwein-Burke-Lewis and Rubinov-Tuy-Mays; places itself among grey-box works (min-max, l1 manifold sampling) (pp. 5-6).
writing: Motivating industrial story withheld until experiments/discussion; candid labels ('most dangerous' intuition technique); negative results explained from logs (pp. 11, 13-14).
limits_future: Feasibility phase only; strict direction can vanish; sampled T not guaranteed; future: exploit objective trends and balance feasibility vs objective in PB (pp. 11, 13-14).

title: Optimization of stochastic blackboxes with adaptive precision
contribution: Introduces MpMads (monotone precision) and DpMads (dynamic precision), MADS variants for blackboxes whose noise level can be tuned at a cost, proves almost-sure Clarke stationarity for any precision-update rule satisfying a minimal condition CDp, redefines profiles in Monte-Carlo draws, and shows DpMads needs about 100x fewer draws than Robust-MADS on an EDF asset-management simulator (read as arXiv 1911.05846v1, 'Optimization of noisy blackboxes with adaptive precision').
problem_entry: Adaptive-precision blackboxes (Monte-Carlo, sigma ~ 1/sqrt(N), cost ~ 1/sigma^2); literature sorted into fixed, monotone and dynamic noise control, with one algorithm placed in each of the last two (pp. 2-3, 5).
key_idea: Inverse-variance ML estimates over a cache; every comparison is a p-value of f(x_c) < f(x_s); precision raised when p is in [beta_l, beta_u] (CDp), kept otherwise for MpMads (CMp); variants differ only in UpdateR so one proof covers both (pp. 4-9).
assumptions: Additive Gaussian noise with x-independent sigma; for the analysis D_f = R^n, bounded level sets, sigma_min = 0, 0 < beta_l <= 0.5, sigma_max finite, CDp; unconstrained (pp. 3, 10-11, 19).
proof_devices: strong law of large numbers -> true minimizer on a finite set eventually minimizes the estimates (Lemma 3.2, p. 12)
p-value convergence via sigma^k <= sigma_max/sqrt(k) (Lemma 3.4, pp. 13-14)
Borel-Cantelli with a max-sum-of-products bound (Lemma 3.1) to keep incumbents in a bounded level set (Thm 3.7, pp. 15-16)
contradiction on finite mesh-intersect-ball, ties handled as random walk on frame sizes (Thm 3.8, pp. 16-17)
refining-direction argument for Clarke stationarity almost surely (Thm 3.9, p. 18)
experiments: Python DpMads/MpMads vs Robust-MADS (NOMAD 3.9.1); currency = Monte-Carlo draws 1/sigma^2 with rebuilt performance/data/accuracy profiles; Norm2 and Moustache (500 runs each); EDF VME asset management (5 integer dates, sigma=1800 at 2^10 draws, sigma_min set to 50) with deterministic MADS and Robust-MADS at fixed draws (32 min to 25.3 days) (pp. 19-27).
positioning: Generalizes Polak-Wetter's monotone-precision GPS (MpMads) and joins Picheny et al.-style dynamic precision (DpMads); contrasts with Robust-MADS, StoMADS, ASTRO-DF, SNOWPAC (pp. 2-3, 5).
writing: Paradigm taxonomy in the introduction; hypotheses gathered in a bullet summary after the last theorem; plain statement of the theoretical equivalence vs practical difference (pp. 2-3, 19, 27).
limits_future: Ad hoc parameters; monotone strategy can explode cost; dynamic strategy weak on flat objectives; per-iteration precision updates; future: constraints with adaptive-precision noise, non-Gaussian noise, models (p. 28).

title: Using symbolic calculations to determine largest small polygons
contribution: Re-derives the largest small hexagon via a complex-plane formulation that factors a degree-14 (not 40) polynomial, re-proves its axial symmetry by symmetrization, and, under the axial-symmetry conjecture, obtains the first algebraic value of the largest small octagon as a root of a degree-42 integer polynomial extracted from a degree-344 discriminant (read as GERAD G-2019-57).
problem_entry: Classic extremal geometry with known cases (odd n, n=4, n=6 via Graham's degree-40 factorization) and only numerical octagon values; entry is a new formulation lowering algebraic degree (pp. 4-5).
key_idea: Fix the pending edge at 0 and i in the complex plane, write area and cycle closure as polynomials, and eliminate variables by resultants and discriminants (Maple), isolating the root with regular-polygon and circle bounds (pp. 6-9).
assumptions: Foster-Szabo diameter-graph theorem and Reinhardt's perpendicularity; octagon result conditional on axial symmetry conjecture (pp. 4-6, 8).
proof_devices: symmetrization-by-averaging contradiction: replace asymmetric angles by their mean, keep diameter 1, strictly gain a triangle's area (Thm 2.1, p. 6)
critical value A of polynomial t => discriminant of t(x)-A vanishes (p. 7)
successive resultant/discriminant elimination to a univariate polynomial in A, then factorization (pp. 7, 9)
root isolation with a priori bounds [0.6, pi/4] and [0.7, pi/4] (pp. 7, 9)
experiments: none beyond computing effort: negligible (hexagon), ~90 s and 100 MB (octagon), decagon failed with 100 GB (p. 9).
positioning: Improves on Graham/Johnson and Lazard for the hexagon; re-proves Yuan's symmetry; turns the 2002 Audet-Hansen-Messine-Xiong numeric octagon and Henrion-Messine bounds into an algebraic value (pp. 5, 9-10).
writing: Very short; conjecture stated inside the theorem; first-analytical-solution claim bounded by the symmetry assumption (pp. 8-9).
limits_future: Conditional on the symmetry conjecture; does not scale to the decagon (memory) (p. 9).

title: Combining cross-entropy and MADS methods for inequality constrained global optimization
contribution: Adds a cross-entropy (CE) Search step to MADS with progressive barrier, drawing elites from the whole cache ranked by PB dominance, triggering the step when elite spread shrinks; calibrated on 100 analytic problems and shown better than GA/DE/CMA-ES/PSO on 19 unconstrained problems and than MADS, LH-MADS and VNS-MADS on MDO, STYRENE and LOCKWOOD (read as arXiv 2012.10173v2).
problem_entry: Two blackbox difficulties (cost, multiple local minima); global heuristics need many evaluations and lack constraint handling, MADS add-ons improve efficiency but not escape; CE is fast to promising regions but unguaranteed and slow to refine (p. 2).
key_idea: CE as a mesh-projected MADS Search: elites from the cache ranked by a PB-dominance Best() function, initialization at poll centre with sigma = 2(u - l) and artificial bounds, truncated normal with alpha = 0.7 smoothing, launched only when ||sigma^k|| < ||sigma^p||, restart when infeasible (pp. 8-10).
assumptions: Bound plus inequality constraints, extended-real f and c; convergence inherited from MADS-PB (bounded trial points -> Clarke stationarity on hypertangent directions if feasible limit) (pp. 2, 4-5).
proof_devices: none new: convergence inherited because the CE Search proposes finitely many mesh points (p. 1, p. 3)
experiments: Calibration on 100 analytic problems (69 unconstrained, 25 constrained, 6 large; 1000(n+1) evals, 3 seeds; NOMAD 3.9.1 + NM, no models); vs pymoo GA/DE/CMA-ES/PSO on 19 unconstrained problems (5 seeds, 3000 evals); MDO, STYRENE, LOCKWOOD with 20 starts x 3 seeds vs MADS, LH-MADS, VNS-MADS; data profiles; feasibility counts (LOCKWOOD 60/60 vs 41/60 and 46/60) (pp. 10-17).
positioning: Contrasts guarantee-free global heuristics (CMA-ES, GA, DE, PSO) with MADS add-ons (VNS, LHS, surrogates, quadratic models, NM); adapts Kroese et al.'s continuous CE, replacing its penalty by PB dominance (pp. 2, 8).
writing: Two aims stated in the introduction (global exploration, preserved guarantees); candid self-assessment that beating heuristics on engineering problems is 'not particularly relevant' (pp. 2, 18).
limits_future: CE not useful at large n (50-60) and unconfirmed on large engineering problems; future: link mesh size to CE standard deviation (pp. 11, 18).
